mainTopic: Tying נזירות to body parts, and whether a husband's הפרה uproots his wife's vow or only cuts it off
overview: The גמרא first raises a contradiction from a ברייתא: tying נזירות to a body part that life does not depend on, like a hand or foot, means nothing. So how can 'my hair is like his hair' make someone a נזיר? רב יהודה answers that the speaker meant to take on the real rules of נזירות, no wine and no haircuts. The גמרא then quotes the משנה's case of a husband who says 'And I' to his wife's vow and can no longer cancel it. This leads to a big question: does a husband's הפרה uproot the vow from the start (מיעקר עקר), or only cut it off from now on (מיגז גייז)? The practical difference is a friend who joined the wife's vow. The גמרא tries three proofs: the 'And I' case, the woman's חטאת that must die, and the woman who gets lashes for breaking her נזירות. Each proof is pushed back with another explanation. The last rejection, about the wording of the משנה's next clause, finishes on the next amud.

steps.title: A teaching about body parts seems to contradict the hair case
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that tying נזירות to a body part that life does not depend on accomplishes nothing. That seems to clash with the earlier ruling that saying 'my hair is like his hair' makes a person a נזיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: They pointed out a contradiction: If someone says 'My hand is a נזיר' or 'My foot is a נזיר,' his words mean nothing. If he says 'My head is a נזיר' or 'My liver is a נזיר,' he is a נזיר. The rule is: if he names something that life depends on, he is a נזיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to clash with the earlier case where someone tied his נזירות to his hair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא sets a clear test: נזירות works only if you name a body part you cannot live without, like the head or liver. Hair is not needed for life. So by this rule, 'my hair is like his hair' should not make a person a נזיר at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And they pointed out a contradiction
is a נזיר (the same form is used for every body part in the list)
my liver
This is the general rule
life depends on it

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
"My hand is a nazirite" and "My foot is a nazirite"
he has not said anything;
"My head is a nazirite," "My liver is a nazirite"
he is a nazirite.

phrases.aramaic: זֶה הַכְּלָל: דָּבָר שֶׁהַנְּשָׁמָה תְּלוּיָה בּוֹ
phrases.english: This is the principle: something upon which life depends
he is a nazirite.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling from just before this point that 'my hair is like his hair' makes a person a נזיר.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that tying oneself to another's נזירות through 'my hair is like his hair' works.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says only body parts that life depends on can carry נזירות. Hair is not one of them, so the hair statement should mean nothing.

steps.title: He meant to take on the rules of wine and hair
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that the hair case works because the person meant, 'Let my mouth be like his mouth for wine, and my hair like his hair for cutting.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: It is a case where he meant this: 'Let my mouth be like his mouth in staying away from wine, and my hair like his hair in not being cut.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the contradiction by explaining what the person really meant when he spoke about his hair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the person tried to make a body part itself 'holy' as a נזיר, and that only works with a vital part. Here, the person was not making his hair a נזיר. He was taking on the actual rules of נזירות (no wine, no haircuts) by comparing himself to the other נזיר, and that is a real acceptance of נזירות.

keyTerms.meaning: that he said (meant) like this
let it be made
like his mouth
from cutting (hair)

steps.whatToRemember: Naming a body part as a נזיר works only for a vital part. Taking on the rules of נזירות (wine and hair) by comparing yourself to another נזיר always works.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: It is where he said like this:
Let my mouth be like his mouth regarding wine,
and my hair like his hair regarding cutting.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the speaker's words are read as accepting the rules of נזירות, not as making a body part a נזיר.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'My hair is like his hair' looked like making the hair itself a נזיר, which fails because life does not depend on hair.
steps.terutzMaskana: He meant to take on the rules of wine and hair like the other נזיר, so he is a נזיר.

steps.title: The משנה's case of a husband who says 'And I'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: if a wife vows נזירות and her husband hears and says 'And I,' he can no longer cancel her vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a woman said 'I am a נזירה,' and her husband heard and said 'And I,' he cannot cancel her vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. It is setting up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying 'And I,' the husband joined his own נזירות onto hers, and the משנה rules that he can no longer cancel her vow. The משנה does not give a reason. The גמרא argues about it later: step 6 says canceling would uproot his own vow too, and step 7 says his 'And I' counts as upholding hers.

keyTerms.meaning: I am hereby a נזירה (a female נזיר)
And I (I accept the same vow)
to cancel (a wife's or daughter's vow)

phrases.english: "I am hereby a nazirite,"
and her husband heard and said "And I"
he cannot nullify.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲרֵינִי נְזִירָה וְשָׁמַע בַּעְלָהּ וַאֲמַר וַאֲנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new section of the סוגיא, quoting the next part of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A husband who joins his wife's נזירות vow by saying 'And I' can no longer cancel it.

steps.title: Does a husband's cancellation uproot the vow or cut it off?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a husband's הפרה erases the vow as if it never existed, or only ends it from now on. It then asks what practical difference this makes.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: Does a husband uproot the vow, or perhaps he only cuts it off? What difference does it make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about how הפרה works. It then asks for a practical case where the answer would matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to picture הפרה. 'Uprooting' (מיעקר עקר) would mean the vow is erased back to the start. 'Cutting' (מיגז גייז) would mean the vow was real until the husband canceled it and stops only from then on. The גמרא wants a case where these two views give different results.

keyTerms.meaning: It was asked of them (a question was raised)
he uproots it (from the very beginning)
he cuts it off (from now on)
What practical difference does it make?

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with התרת נדרים by a חכם. Here the question is only about how a husband's הפרה works.

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
Does a husband uproot (the vow),
or perhaps he cuts it off?
phrases.notes: 'Cutting' means the vow counted until now and ends only from this moment.

phrases.english: For what does it make a difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the subject of a husband canceling his wife's vow, which the משנה just raised.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a husband's הפרה works from the beginning (uprooting) or only from now on (cutting), and in what case that would matter.

steps.title: The practical difference: a friend who said 'And I'
steps.stepSummary: A friend joins the wife's vow by saying 'And I,' and then the wife's husband cancels the wife's vow. If הפרה uproots, the friend is free too. If it only cuts, the friend stays a נזירה. The גמרא then asks: which is it? The next steps try to answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference is a woman who vowed נזירות, and her friend heard and said 'And I,' and then the first woman's husband heard and canceled her vow. If you say he uproots, the friend is also released. If you say he only cuts it off, the wife is released but her friend is still bound. So which is it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers 'what difference does it make' with a case of two women. It then repeats the question: which view is right?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The friend's vow rests on the wife's vow. If הפרה erases the wife's vow from the start, the friend attached herself to nothing, so her vow falls away. If הפרה only ends the vow from now, the wife's vow was real when the friend joined, so the friend stays a נזירה even though the wife is freed.

keyTerms.meaning: her friend
and he canceled (her vow) for her
is released (the vow is dissolved)
is bound (still forbidden)

steps.whyThisMatters: This case shows clearly how the two views of הפרה work: one looks back to the start of the vow, the other works only from now on. That idea comes up again in other areas of vows.

phrases.english: For a woman who vowed to be a nazirite,
and her friend heard and said "And I,"

phrases.aramaic: וְשָׁמַע בַּעְלָהּ שֶׁל רִאשׁוֹנָה וְהֵפֵר לָהּ.
phrases.english: and the husband of the first woman heard and nullified for her.
If you say he uproots,
that one is also released.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the friend. Her vow was attached to a vow that is now treated as if it never existed.

phrases.english: And if you say he cuts it off,
she is released; her friend is bound.
What is it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers 'what difference does it make' from step 4, then asks the main question again.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference shows up with a friend who said 'And I' to the wife's vow. Uprooting frees the friend too. Cutting frees only the wife and leaves the friend bound.

steps.title: A proof from the 'And I' case that the husband uproots
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא uses the משנה of the husband who said 'ואני' to try to prove that הפרה uproots the vow from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if she said 'I am a נזירה' and her husband heard and said 'And I,' he cannot annul. Now if the husband only cuts the vow off from now on, let him annul it for his wife while he himself stays bound. So doesn't this prove the husband uproots the vow?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the open question by pointing to the משנה about the husband who said 'ואני.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: If הפרה only cut the vow off from now on, her vow was fully real when he joined it. He could annul hers and still stay a נזיר himself, so nothing would stop him. Since the משנה says he cannot annul, it must be that annulling would uproot her vow and his own along with it, and that is why he is blocked.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And I': the words someone says to join another person's nezirus
If it enters your mind: if you were to think that...
The husband uproots: his הפרה erases the vow as if it never existed
The husband cuts: his הפרה only ends the vow from now on

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"I am hereby a nezirah"
phrases.notes: This is the משנה quoted back in Step 3.

phrases.english: and her husband heard and said "And I"
he cannot annul.
And if it should enter your mind
that the husband cuts off the vow from now on,
let him annul it for his wife
and he himself stays bound.
Rather, isn't it learned from this
that the husband uproots the vow?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הֲרֵינִי נְזִירָה וְשָׁמַע בַּעְלָהּ וְאָמַר וַאֲנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to resolve the question left open in Step 5 by bringing a משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That הפרה uproots the vow retroactively (מיעקר עקר).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: a husband who said 'ואני' to his wife's nezirus cannot annul it.

steps.title: Rejecting the proof: 'And I' counts as upholding the vow
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the husband may still only cut the vow. He cannot annul because saying 'ואני' is like upholding her vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, really he only cuts, and in principle he should be able to annul for her. The reason he can't is that saying 'And I' is like saying 'It is upheld for you.' If he asks a חכם to release his upholding, he can annul. If not, he can't.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. It gives a different reason why the husband can't annul, one that has nothing to do with uprooting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By joining her vow, the husband showed he approves of it. That counts as הקמה, and once a husband upholds a vow he loses the right to annul it. So the משנה tells us nothing about cutting versus uprooting, and the question is open again.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really: the original view still stands
'It is upheld for you': the husband confirming his wife's vow
Upholding: the husband confirms the vow, which takes away his power to annul it
Asks a חכם to release a vow or commitment

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the husband can never annul after saying 'ואני.' The block comes only from his הקמה. If a חכם releases that, he can annul again.

phrases.english: No, really he cuts off the vow from now on.
And by right he should be able to annul it for her.
And this is the reason he cannot annul:
since he said to her "And I,"
it is as if he said "It is upheld for you."
If he asks for a release from his upholding, he can annul,
and if not, he cannot annul.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 6 by giving another reason for the משנה's ruling.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof only. It does not prove the opposite side; it just shows the משנה fits both views.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed uprooting was the only reason the husband can't annul. Really, his 'ואני' counts as הקמה, which blocks annulment no matter which view is right.

steps.title: A second source: the woman who set aside an animal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה about a woman who set aside an animal for her נזירות offerings before her husband annulled her vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a woman vowed to be a נזירה and set aside her animal, and afterward her husband annulled her vow. If the animal was his, it goes out and grazes with the flock. If the animal was hers, the חטאת must be left to die.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new משנה to try again to answer the question. This step sets up the source; the next step draws the proof from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rulings matter here. If the animal was the husband's, it never became holy at all and goes back to the flock. If it was hers, the animal set aside as a חטאת is treated as truly holy, so it must die, like any חטאת that cannot be brought.

keyTerms.meaning: She set aside an animal for a קרבן
It grazes with the flock: it is treated as a regular animal
Sin-offering, one of the קרבנות a נזיר brings at the end
It must die: it is left alone until it dies, because it is holy but cannot be offered

phrases.english: Come and hear: A woman who vowed to be a nazirite
and set aside her animal,
and afterward her husband annulled her vow:
if the animal was his,
it goes out and grazes with the flock.
And if the animal was hers,
the sin-offering must die.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁנָּדְרָה בְּנָזִיר, וְהִפְרִישָׁה אֶת בְּהֶמְתָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected, the גמרא brings a different source to the same question.
steps.raayaObject: Sets up a proof for one side of the cut-or-uproot question.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about a woman whose husband annulled her נזירות after she set aside an animal.

steps.title: The animal that must die proves the husband only cuts
steps.stepSummary: Since her חטאת must die instead of becoming ordinary, her vow must have been real when she set it aside. So the husband only cuts the vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think the husband uproots the vow, the animal should just go out as ordinary! So doesn't this prove that the husband only cuts the vow?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the proof from the משנה it just quoted, this time for the opposite side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If הפרה uprooted the vow, she was never a נזירה, and her animal should simply become חולין. The משנה instead treats the animal as truly holy and makes it die. That means she really was a נזירה when she set it aside, so the husband only cut the vow off from then on.

keyTerms.meaning: It should go out as ordinary (non-holy) property
Ordinary, non-holy things

steps.whatToRemember: First proof (the 'ואני' case) was rejected, because 'ואני' counts as הקמה. Second proof: a חטאת that must die seems to show the vow was real at the time, which would point to בעל מיגז גייז. The next step rejects this proof as well.
steps.whyThisMatters: The two proofs pull in opposite directions. This shows how the practical outcome for a קרבן can reveal what kind of thing הפרה is.

phrases.english: And if it should enter your mind
that the husband uproots the vow,
the animal should go out as ordinary!
Rather, isn't it learned from this
that the husband only cuts off the vow!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ בַּעַל מִיעְקָר עָקַר — תִּיפּוֹק לְחוּלִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the actual proof from the משנה quoted in Step 8.
steps.raayaObject: That הפרה only cuts the vow from now on (מיגז גייז).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling that her חטאת must die, which shows the animal was truly holy and the vow was real when she set it aside.

steps.title: The sin-offering dies for a different reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 9. The husband may really uproot the vow. Her חטאת still dies, because it is treated like a חטאת whose owners have died.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, I can tell you that the husband uproots the vow. Here is the reason her animal dies: since she no longer needs atonement, the animal is like a sin-offering whose owners died, and we have a tradition that such a sin-offering must be left to die.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last proof. It shows that the חטאת dying does not prove the vow was ever real.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof in step 9 said: the חטאת dies, so the vow must have been real. Now the גמרא gives another reason for the animal to die. Once the woman needs no כפרה, her animal falls into the known category of a חטאת whose owners have died, and by tradition such an animal is left to die. So the ruling fits מיעקר עקר too.

keyTerms.meaning: He uproots it, meaning the vow is erased from the very beginning
Atonement, which a קרבן brings
A sin-offering whose owners have died. It cannot be brought and is left to die.
We have learned it as a tradition passed down

steps.confusionAlert: The animal dying does not have to mean the vow was real. The גמרא is showing that the same ruling has another possible reason.

phrases.english: Really, I can tell you
the husband uproots the vow,
and this is the reason:
since she does not need atonement,
it is like a sin-offering whose owners have died,
and we have a tradition that a sin-offering whose owners died must die.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ בַּעַל מִיעְקָר עָקַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from the woman's חטאת in step 9
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof itself. It does not prove that the husband uproots.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The חטאת dying can be explained by the rule of a חטאת whose owners died, even if the vow is uprooted.

steps.title: A new source: the woman who broke her נזירות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: a woman who vowed נזירות and then drank wine and became טמאה to the dead gets forty lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a woman who vowed to be a נזירה, and was drinking wine and becoming impure from the dead, gets the forty lashes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new משנה to try again to answer the question. This step only quotes the source; the next step will build the proof from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling is that the woman gets מלקות for breaking her נזירות. The proof will depend on what kind of case this is, which the גמרא figures out next.

keyTerms.meaning: She receives the forty lashes (מלקות) for breaking a Torah prohibition
Making herself impure through contact with the dead, which a נזיר may not do

phrases.english: Come and hear:
a woman who vowed to be a nazirite,
and she was drinking wine
and becoming impure from the dead —
she receives the forty lashes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the חטאת proof fell away, a new source is brought for the same open question
steps.raayaObject: That the husband only cuts the vow (מיגז גייז)
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of the woman who vowed נזירות and broke it

steps.title: The lashes prove the husband only cuts
steps.stepSummary: The משנה must be talking about a case where the husband annulled the vow. She still gets lashes, so the vow was real until he annulled it. That means he only cuts it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the husband did not annul her vow, does this need to be said? Rather, it is obvious that the husband annulled it. And if you think the husband uproots the vow, why does she get forty lashes? So must we not learn from this that the husband only cuts the vow?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא works out the case of the משנה and uses it to prove that הפרה only cuts the vow from now on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the vow were never annulled, it would be obvious that she gets lashes, like any נזיר who breaks the rules. So the משנה must mean the husband annulled it afterward. If annulling erased the vow from the start, her drinking would not have been a sin at all. Since she still gets lashes, the vow must have been real when she drank.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? A request to define the exact situation
Does it need to be said? Meaning it would be too obvious to teach
He annulled the vow (from הפרה)
He cuts it, meaning the vow ends only from now on

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a strong-looking proof, because מלקות requires a real sin at the time she acted.

phrases.english: What is the case?
If we say the husband did not annul it for her —
does that need to be said?
Rather, it is obvious that the husband annulled it for her.
And if you think
the husband uproots the vow —
why does she get forty lashes?
Rather, must we not learn from this
that the husband only cuts the vow?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds the proof out of the משנה quoted in step 11
steps.raayaObject: הפרה only cuts the vow (מיגז גייז)
steps.raayaSupportSource: She gets lashes even though her husband annulled the vow, so the vow was real when she drank

steps.title: The wording comes from the next clause
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to reject the proof. The husband may still uproot the vow. The first clause is worded this way because of the next clause, which says she does not get lashes if he annulled the vow without her knowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, I can tell you the husband uproots the vow. It is worded this way because the next clause teaches: if her husband annulled it and she did not know, and she was drinking wine and becoming impure from the dead, she does not get the forty lashes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to push back on the proof by pointing to the next part of the same משנה. Its full explanation continues in the lines after this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof in step 12 rested on one assumption: the first clause must be about an annulled vow, because otherwise it would be too obvious to teach. The גמרא's answer, which finishes on the next amud, is that the first clause really is the plain case where the husband never annulled. It is taught only to match the second clause, where he annulled without her knowing and she does not get forty lashes. So the first clause says nothing about annulment, and מיעקר עקר still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, I can tell you. Used to keep the original view and reject a proof
The latter clause of a משנה
And she did not know that her vow had been annulled

steps.confusionAlert: This text stops in the middle of the גמרא's answer. The point about the סיפא is finished in the next lines.

phrases.english: Really, I can tell you
the husband uproots the vow,
and it is because the latter clause teaches:

phrases.aramaic: הֵיפֵר לָהּ בַּעְלָהּ וְהִיא לֹא יָדְעָה,
phrases.english: if her husband annulled it for her and she did not know,
and she was drinking wine
and becoming impure from the dead —
she does not get the forty lashes,

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ בַּעַל מִיעְקָר עָקַר וּמִשּׁוּם דְּקָתָנֵי סֵיפָא

steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Step 12 assumed the רישא must involve הפרה because the plain case is too obvious to teach. Really, the רישא is the plain case with no הפרה, stated only to set up the contrast with the סיפא. So it proves nothing about cutting versus uprooting.
